title: Exam Questions
text:
Instructions
This exam has 4 questions, 10 points each. All necessary data files for this exam are uploaded to Canvas. You will use Quarto (.qmd) document to work on the question. When you finish, please upload both your .qmd and rendered .html files to the “Midterm Exam” assignment submission link on Canvas.
You have 90 minutes to complete the exam from 9:30AM to 11:00AM.
Start your work in a Quarto document. To ensure that your rendered HTML includes all image outputs, copy and edit the following into your YAML header:
title: "Exam Answers"
author: "<Your Name>"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  warning: false
For the questions, please write out all your code you used, and include a clear final answer to a question. If you didn’t complete a section, describe your problem-solving approach instead, i.e. explain what you intended to do and your reasoning.


Question 1: Cleaning and Transforming
You are given q1_forest_area.csv, which records the forest area of 80 countries over time. Each row is one country in one year. It has four columns:

country: Country name
code: 3-letter country code
year: Year of the record
forest_area_ha: Forest area in hectares

Questions:

Filter the data for Angola. How many years of records does Angola have, and what are the first and last years? Then do the same for Belgium. (1 point)
Not every country has a record for every year. Create one summary table that counts the number of years recorded for each country. Using this table, list all countries with fewer than 31 years of records. (2 points)
Back to the original table, for the year 2020 only, which 3 countries have the largest forest area? (2 points)
Use the original table, keep only the years 1990 and 2020, then use a pivot function to reshape the data so that each country is one row, with one column for 1990 forest area and one column for 2020 forest area. Call this table forest_wide. (2.5 points)
Using forest_wide, calculate the change in forest area from 1990 to 2020. Which country had the largest decrease in forest area during the 30 years? (2.5 points)


Data source: Forests and Deforestation in Our World in Data. Adapted dataset from TidyTuesday 2021-15 Global Deforestation.




Question 2: Summarizing and Plotting
Bluebikes is Metro Boston’s public bike share program. You are given a Bluebikes ridership dataset q2_bike_trips.csv. Each row represents a single trip, including its start time (started_at), end time (ended_at), start station, end station, and rider type (member_casual: "member" or "casual"). The dataset covers all trips taken on Wednesday, September 9, 2026, the first day of our fall semester.
Q2.1

Filter for all trips that started at the station “MIT at Mass Ave / Amherst St”. Save the result as a new table, e.g. mit_trips. (1 point)
The last two columns of the data, started_hour and ended_hour, give the hour (0-23) in which each trip started and ended. Using started_hour, create a line graph that shows the number of trips by hour at this station, with two lines: one for member riders and one for casual riders. Include a title and x-axis tick labels by hour. (7 points)

Your graph may look similar (but not the same!) as the following example. Your theme, color and text choices can be different.

Q2.2 Continue using mit_trips (all trips that started at “MIT at Mass Ave / Amherst St”).

Create a table that shows how many trips ended at each station, by counting end_station_id. Keep only the end stations with more than 1 trip (i.e., n > 1). You will use this result in Question 3. (2 point)


Data source: Bluebikes System Data. (2026). Bluebikes Comprehensive Trip Histories.




Question 3: Combining and Mapping
You are also provided a Bluebikes station dataset q3_bike_stations.csv, which includes station names (NAME), ids (Number), locations (Lat, Long), and total docks at each station.

Join your result from Q2.2 (end stations with more than 1 trip) with the station dataset, matching on station id. Your result should have 53 rows (2 points)
Using the sf package, map these trip counts using the stations’ geographic locations. (8 points)

Remove any stations without valid location information (Long, or Lat) after the join.
Convert the joined data to an sf object.
Use point size to show the number of trips ending at each station (as one aes() argument).
Use q3_basemap.geojson as your base map.
Include a title and a legend.


Your map may look similar (but not the same!) as the following example. Your theme, color and text choices can be different.


Data source: Bluebikes System Data. (2026). Bluebikes Stations. Analyze Boston. (2026). Boston neighborhood boundary.




Question 4: Census Data Collection
In this question you will use the tidycensus package to collect American Community Survey (ACS) data. The following code is meant to download the number of occupied housing units and renter-occupied housing units for every census tract in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, from the most recent ACS 5-year estimates.

Fill in the missing variables argument so the code runs correctly. Look for table B25003: Tenure. (4 points)
Using your result of API call, calculate rate that equals renter-occupied housing units divided by total occupied housing units, so that we have renter rate for each tract. (6 points)


library(tidycensus)

tenure <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "MA",
  county = "Middlesex",
  variables = ,
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5"
)



🎉THIS IS THE END OF THE EXAM 🎉

Question 2: Summarizing and Plotting

biketrips <- read_csv("data/q2_bike_trips.csv")


Q2.1 Trips by hour at MIT at Mass Ave / Amherst St
There are 355 trips starting at this station.

mit_trips <-
  biketrips |>
  filter(start_station_name == "MIT at Mass Ave / Amherst St")


mit_trips |>
  count(started_hour, member_casual) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = started_hour, y = n, color = member_casual)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 1))+
  labs(x = "Hour", y = "Number of Trips Started", color = "Rider Type",
       title = "All Trips from MIT at Mass Ave / Amherst St",
       subtitle = "September 9, 2026") +
  theme_minimal()










Q2.2 Count trips by end station, filter >1
53 end stations have more than 1 trip.

mit_end <-
  mit_trips |>
  count(end_station_id) |>
  filter(n > 1)

title: Exam Answer Key
text:
Question 3 Combining and Mapping

station <- read_csv("data/q3_bike_stations.csv")
basemap <- st_read("data/q3_basemap.geojson")

1 Join trips by station id

# Join trips by end station to the station data
station_joined <-
  left_join(mit_end, station,
            by = c("end_station_id" = "Number"))

2 Convert to spatial data

# Remove stations without valid location, then convert to spatial data
station_sf <-
  station_joined |>
  filter(!is.na(Long)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Long", "Lat"), crs = 4326)

3 Map

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = basemap, fill = "white")+
  geom_sf(data = station_sf, aes(size = n), color = "red", alpha = 0.4)+
    labs(size = "Trip Count",
         title = "All Trips from MIT at Mass Ave / Amherst St",
         subtitle = "End stations with more than 1 trip, September 9, 2026")+
  theme_void()

title: Exam Answer Key
text:
Question 4: Census Data Collection
Q4.1 Fill in variables with total occupied housing units (B25003_001) and renter-occupied housing units (B25003_003). Naming the variables is optional but makes the next step easier.

library(tidycensus)

tenure <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "MA",
  county = "Middlesex",
  variables = c(total = "B25003_001", renter = "B25003_003"),
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Q4.2 Add output = "wide" to get_acs() and use renterE / totalE directly. Alternatively, pivot to wide before dividing.

# Option 1 Add output = "wide
tenure_rate <- 
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    state = "MA",
    county = "Middlesex",
    variables = c(total = "B25003_001", renter = "B25003_003"),
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide") |> 
  mutate(rate = renterE / totalE)

# Option 2 Pivot to wide before dividing
tenure_rate <-
  tenure |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  mutate(rate = renter / total)
